source_title: NVIDIA-NeMo/Switchyard: Switchyard lets LLM applications route traffic across models and providers while preserving native OpenAI and Anthropic API compatibility - enabling flexible model selection, benchmarking, and cost/performance optimization. - GitHub
source_excerpt:
Switchyard is an open-source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. It combines efficient models with more capable models so you can balance task success, cost, and latency on your workload.
Adopt Switchyard by embedding its Rust core, libsy , in your gateway or agent harness. You own the model clients, credentials, and service. Switchyard supplies the routing decision.
Quickstart · Documentation · Benchmarks · What’s new · Roadmap · Releases · Contributing
Configure the models an agent can use and choose a routing algorithm.
The algorithm examines the request or the agent's recent tool activity. Some algorithms call a model to judge the task.
A gateway or agent sends the request to the selected model. Routing can change as the agent continues its work.
Evaluate the complete agent, model pool, and routing configuration against your single-model baseline. A cheaper model call does not guarantee a cheaper successfully completed task. The tuning loop gives the steps for that evaluation, and Troubleshooting lists the settings that disable routing without an error.
Through an existing gateway : Use an available gateway integration.
Embed libsy in your harness : Add libsy to a service you operate.
Evaluate Switchyard locally : Compare routing configurations with your own model pool using the demo server.
Relay 0.8.x and 0.9.0 can lose upstream error status and details when the plugin is enabled, even for models outside its routes. Review the upstream error compatibility note before enabling the plugin.
LiteLLM and NeMo Relay run in your own deployment. Follow each gateway's guidance for credentials and service operation.
Algorithm::run_stream hands model calls and the final routing outcome back to your application. In this development-API outline, comments mark the work your code supplies:
Inputs: supply an algorithm, model pool, request, and state.
Calls: your clients handle model calls. Stage returns a selection; other algorithms may return an answer.
Start here: Rust quickstart · Python bindings .
The standalone server is provided only for demos and local evaluation. It is not a supported production deployment path.
Evaluate routing locally with the standalone server and your own model pool, then verify routing is active .
The experimental desktop and terminal quickstart covers local installation, coding-tool connections, sessions, usage, recovery, and uninstall.
Agent-specific guides are available for pi and Oh My Pi .
Start with Auto. Choose Task, Execution, or Composite when you need more control. These names describe routing choices. The configuration keys are unchanged.
Auto is a fixed preset in v0.3.0. It does not compare strategies at runtime. The TOML runner supports type = "auto" . In Rust, use StageRouterConfig::new(PickerMode::EfficientFirst, 0.5) for the same preset.
The routing overview retains the full catalogue, including Plan/Execute , escalation , advisor , sub-agent , and random strategies. Integration support varies: check the gateway guide before choosing an algorithm.
Prefill routing is designed for fast, efficient model selection using a model's prefill activations and a classifier trained on your own evaluation data.
Compare benchmark results and configs for Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE. For latency and routing overhead testing, see Soak Testing .
Benchmark setup and profiles : run your own baseline and routing comparisons.
Mechanics of Libsy : steps, model calls, and routing outcomes.
TOML schema : configuration fields and defaults.
Rust crate reference : core and optional integration crates.
Installation : package and platform requirements.
Pre-1.0 software. APIs, configuration, and routing behavior can change between releases. Pin the version you integrate.
